program: Violence interruption, youth opportunity and community support
priceScope: Full annual recipient cost against conditional partial injury-response and youth-workforce benefits; not whole-portfolio or marginal-gift EV.

what: Struggle of Love provides violence interruption, trauma support and school-based mentorship in Northeast Denver and North Aurora. It also operates food distribution and youth employment opportunities. Its teams connect families to counseling, crisis support and other community providers.
strengths: Local BIPOC-led organization with direct crisis and neighborhood access.
The 2024 report distinguishes shooting incidents, therapy completions and paid youth placements.
Food, employment and mental-health support address more than one pathway to household welfare.
reservations: Incident responses and paid placements do not establish incremental health or earnings gains.
Controlled violence-intervention evidence is uncertain and differs from SOL’s model.
Full annual costs cover several unquantified channels, so the displayed partial-channel reference is not a portfolio ranking.

sections.heading: What the original sources establish
sections.body: The 2024 report describes 105 shooting incidents responded to, 30 therapy completions or successful discharges, 25 concession-employed youth and ten additional public youth-employment placements. Food pounds, STAR referrals and center visits are not unique causal outcomes. None of these categories is added as an independent health cohort.

sections.heading: Health, resources and alternatives
sections.body: The numerical reference hypothesizes one exposed person per shooting incident, 20% recipient contribution, a 5% additional injury-risk reduction and 0.1 QALY per avoided nonfatal injury. These are judgments, not measured SOL effects. A 130-person hospital-based pilot RCT found a 10.4 percentage-point repeat-injury difference with p=.15; a null or harmful result remains plausible. The distinct 25-person concession-workforce envelope uses 30% additional employment and $500 net annual household gain after taxes, benefit withdrawals and ordinary work costs, with $50 additional participation cost on every household and conservative positive overlap. Public placements, alternative jobs, employers and other support organizations matter. There is no child lifetime-wage or retail food-income claim.

sections.heading: Giving and cost boundary
sections.body: The full FY2024 recipient expense is $3,006,875. Therapy, pantry and broader coalition contributions remain unknown, not zero, and the model does not estimate whole-portfolio or next-gift expected value. A $30/hour sensitivity for 3,720 volunteer hours adds shadow resources without asserting a household payer loss. Giving goes through the recipient’s own ColoradoGives link; no donation was executed.

sources.title: Original youth injury pilot randomized trial

model.costScope: Full FY2024 organizational expenses, not allocated injury-response or job-placement costs.
model.geographicAttribution: Northeast Denver and North Aurora service area is within pinned ten-county Denver CBSA19740; .98 recipient-benefit share is a judgment allowing outside residents.
model.formula: Health = incident envelope × patient-per-incident hypothesis × additionality × injury-risk response × finite QALY burden, less full incident-exposure harms. Separate workforce household joint logs include full costs and positive-only overlap; price = 10 × annual cost / (health + signed resource equivalent).
model.counterfactual: Other community, hospital and public violence response; publicly supported youth placements, ordinary jobs and other family resources.
model.attribution: Recipient contribution .2 for injury prevention and job additionality .3 are separate hypotheses; they are not inferred from partner STAR totals.
model.uncertainty: Primary pilot trial does not establish injury reduction; recipient injury severity, unique people, net wages, donor capacity and portfolio cost allocation remain unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: 105 incident responses; 25 concession-employed youth; ten public placements; 30 therapy completions/discharges; 3,720 volunteer hours in the 2024 report.
